content: The Pidgeon process is a method for producing magnesium metal through silicothermic reduction. This process requires approximately 35-40 MWh of energy per ton of magnesium produced, which is comparable to molten salt electrolytic methods but significantly higher than the theoretical minimum energy requirement of 7 MWh per ton. In this process, silicon reacts with magnesium oxide (magnesia) to produce silica and magnesium. Although this reaction is thermodynamically unfavorable according to Ellingham diagrams, it can be driven forward by applying heat and removing magnesium vapor as it forms. Vacuum is preferred because it allows the reaction to occur at lower temperatures. The silicon used in this process is typically in the form of ferrosilicon, an inexpensive alloy. The iron in ferrosilicon does not participate in the reaction and acts as a spectator. The magnesium oxide used in the Pidgeon process can be derived from various sources. One method involves extracting magnesium chloride from seawater or lake water, hydrolyzing it to magnesium hydroxide, and then calcining it to magnesium oxide by removing water. Another method uses mined magnesite (MgCO3), which is calcined to magnesium oxide by removing carbon dioxide. However, the most commonly used raw material is dolomite, a mixed calcium-magnesium carbonate (Ca,Mg)CO3. When dolomite is calcined, the calcium oxide formed in the reaction zone reacts with silica, releasing heat and consuming one of the reaction products, which helps drive the equilibrium toward magnesium production. The Pidgeon process is a batch process. Finely powdered calcined dolomite and ferrosilicon are mixed, pressed into briquettes, and placed into retorts made of nickel-chrome-steel alloy. The reaction zone of the retort is heated using gas, coal, or electricity, while the condensing section, which extends out of the furnace, is water-cooled and equipped with removable baffles. Magnesium vapor is distilled and condensed into high-purity magnesium crowns, which are then remelted and cast into ingots. Using carbon as a reducing agent instead of silicon is not feasible in this process. This is because silicon dioxide is a solid, while carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are gaseous. These gaseous byproducts would follow the magnesium vapor and reverse the reaction, leading to the reformation of the initial reactants. Although a process involving shock-freezing of the vapors to prevent the reverse reaction has been proposed, it is not economically viable for industrial use. At lower temperatures (600-700°C), where magnesium is still liquid or solid but carbon oxides are gaseous, the thermodynamic forces opposing the reaction are too strong, making the process impractical. Additionally, silicon is a more effective reducing agent than carbon because silicon dioxide has a much higher heat of formation compared to carbon oxides, as shown in Ellingham diagrams. The Pidgeon process was invented in the early 1940s by Dr. Lloyd Montgomery Pidgeon of the Canadian National Research Council. The first plant using this method was built in 1941 in Haley, Ontario, Canada, and operated for 63 years, most recently by Timminco Metals. Over the past decade, the Pidgeon process has become the dominant method for magnesium production worldwide, with China being the leading producer, relying almost exclusively on this method. Before the mid-1990s, magnesium production was dominated by electrolytic processes, with the United States as the primary supplier. Dow Chemical operated a large plant near Freeport, Texas, which produced magnesium through seawater-extracted magnesium chloride electrolysis. As of 2005, the United States has only one magnesium producer, US Magnesium, located in Utah. This company emerged from the now-defunct Magcorp. Severe anti-dumping tariffs have been imposed on Chinese magnesium imports, which has significantly impacted the global market. In 1995, the United States produced 45,000 tons of magnesium annually, accounting for 7% of global production, while China produced only 12,000 tons, or 4%. By 2005, China had become the dominant producer, accounting for 400,000 tons out of the global 615,000 tons, or 65%, while the United States' share remained at 45,000 tons. The price of magnesium dropped from $2,300 per ton in 1995 to $1,300 per ton by 2001 but rose again to over $2,300 per ton by 2004 due to increased costs for ferrosilicon, energy, and transportation, as well as the anticipation of anti-dumping duties. The energy efficiency of the Pidgeon process is comparable to electrolytic methods, with both requiring approximately 35-40 MWh per ton of magnesium. However, the Pidgeon process is less technologically complex and produces high-purity magnesium due to the distillation and vapor deposition conditions. Historically, other major magnesium producers included Norsk Hydro in Norway and Canada, as well as countries in the former Soviet Union, Brazil, and France, which benefited from cheap and abundant hydroelectric or nuclear power. Recently, Israel has entered the magnesium market, and an Australian company, Magnesium International, plans to build a 100,000-ton-per-year smelter in Sokhna, Egypt, using the Dow electrolytic process.
